title: Cell specialization
summary: How unspecialized cells from the zygote differentiate, what makes stem cells special, why cell size is limited by surface area to volume ratio, and how pneumocytes, muscle cells and gametes are adapted to their jobs.

keyterms.definition: Development of an unspecialized cell into a specialized cell by expressing some genes and not others; all cells keep the same genome.
Signalling molecule whose concentration gradient gives embryonic cells positional information, influencing which genes they express.
Unspecialized cell that can divide repeatedly (self-renewal) and can differentiate into one or more specialized cell types.
Location in the body where stem cells are maintained and their division and differentiation are controlled, e.g. bone marrow and hair follicles.
Able to differentiate into any cell type, including extra-embryonic cells such as placenta, e.g. the zygote and very early embryo cells.
Able to differentiate into any type of body cell but not a whole organism, e.g. embryonic stem cells.
Able to differentiate into only a limited range of related cell types, e.g. adult stem cells in bone marrow.
Ratio of a cell's membrane area to its volume; it decreases as cells grow, limiting exchange relative to metabolic needs.
Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane that increase surface area for absorption, e.g. in proximal convoluted tubule cells.
Extremely thin, flattened alveolar cell covering most of the alveolar surface, minimizing gas diffusion distance.
Cuboidal alveolar cell that secretes surfactant, reducing surface tension so alveoli do not collapse.
Junction between branched cardiac muscle cells allowing electrical impulses to pass rapidly so the cells contract together.
Very long, multinucleate skeletal muscle 'cell' formed by fusion of cells; an atypical cell structure.
Cap on the sperm head containing enzymes that digest the zona pellucida around the egg.

questions.prompt: How do the unspecialized cells of an early embryo begin to develop into different cell types?
options: Each cell receives a different set of genes during mitosis
Morphogen gradients give cells positional information, so they express different genes
Cells lose the genes they do not need
Cells in contact with the uterus become totipotent
questions.explanation: Cells at different positions experience different morphogen concentrations, which switch on different genes and set them on different pathways of differentiation. Their genomes stay the same.

questions.statement: Different specialized cells in the body contain different genes.
questions.explanation: Almost all body cells contain the same genome; differentiation results from differences in gene expression, not from losing or gaining genes.

questions.text: Signalling chemicals whose concentration gradients tell embryonic cells their position are called ___.
questions.explanation: A cell's response depends on the morphogen concentration it detects, so cells along a gradient differentiate in different ways.

questions.prompt: Which two properties together define a stem cell?
options: It is large and contains many mitochondria
It has no nucleus and divides by meiosis
It is found only in embryos and can form any cell
It can divide repeatedly (self-renewal) and can differentiate into specialized cells
questions.explanation: Stem cells maintain their own population by dividing endlessly while also producing cells that differentiate. Adult stem cells exist too, so they are not limited to embryos.

questions.prompt: Match each type of cell to its potency.

pairs.right: Zygote: can form any cell, including placenta
Embryonic stem cell: any body cell type
Bone marrow stem cell: a few related types

questions.explanation: Potency decreases as development proceeds: from totipotent zygote, to pluripotent embryonic cells, to multipotent adult stem cells, to specialized cells.

questions.statement: Bone marrow and hair follicles are examples of stem cell niches in adult humans.
questions.explanation: Both contain populations of adult stem cells maintained by their surroundings: bone marrow produces blood cells and hair follicles regenerate hair and skin.

questions.text: Stem cells in the bone ___ divide and differentiate to produce red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
questions.explanation: Bone marrow is a stem cell niche where multipotent haematopoietic stem cells continually replace blood cells.

questions.prompt: Order these cells from greatest to least potency.
questions.explanation: The zygote is totipotent, embryonic stem cells are pluripotent, bone marrow stem cells are multipotent, and a red blood cell is fully differentiated.

questions.prompt: What is the function of a stem cell niche?
options: It provides a microenvironment that maintains stem cells and controls their division and differentiation
It is where specialized cells go to die
It stores spare genes for differentiated cells
It prevents stem cells from ever dividing
questions.explanation: Signals from surrounding cells in the niche keep stem cells unspecialized until more cells are needed, then trigger division and differentiation.

questions.prompt: Why are pluripotent embryonic stem cells of more therapeutic interest than multipotent adult stem cells?
options: They divide more slowly and so are safer
They are found in every adult tissue
They can differentiate into a wider range of cell types
They contain more genes
questions.explanation: Pluripotent cells can become any body cell type, whereas multipotent cells are limited to a few related types, e.g. blood cells.

questions.prompt: Why is there an upper limit on the size of most cells?
options: Larger cells would have too many genes
Larger cells cannot divide by mitosis
As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so exchange cannot keep up with metabolism
As a cell grows, its surface area increases faster than its volume
questions.explanation: Metabolic demand depends on volume but exchange of materials and heat depends on surface area. Volume scales with length cubed and area with length squared, so the SA:V ratio falls as cells grow.

questions.statement: A larger cube has a higher surface area to volume ratio than a smaller cube.
questions.explanation: For a cube of side L, SA:V = 6L²/L³ = 6/L, so the ratio falls as L increases.

questions.prompt: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 2 µm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 µm² and volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 µm³, so the ratio is 24:8 = 3:1.

questions.text: Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane that increase surface area for absorption are called ___.
questions.explanation: Microvilli are tiny folds of a single cell's membrane. Villi are much larger, multicellular projections of the intestinal wall.

questions.prompt: Match each cell to how its size relates to its function.

pairs.right: Large, with food reserves for the early embryo
Small enough to squeeze through capillaries
Axon can be over a metre long

questions.explanation: Cell size is part of specialization: some cells are unusually large or long because of their role, others are small to be mobile or fit narrow spaces.

questions.statement: The biconcave shape of red blood cells increases their surface area to volume ratio.
questions.explanation: Being thin and dished gives a larger surface for oxygen uptake and a short diffusion distance to all of the haemoglobin.

questions.prompt: Which human cell has the largest volume?
options: Red blood cell
Sperm cell
White blood cell
Egg cell (ovum)
questions.explanation: The ovum is about 0.1 mm across, visible to the naked eye, because it carries the cytoplasm and nutrients for the early embryo.

questions.prompt: A cell grows larger without changing shape. Which problem is most likely to arise?
options: Its DNA content doubles automatically
Oxygen cannot diffuse in fast enough to meet the needs of the whole cytoplasm
Its membrane becomes thicker
Its surface area decreases in absolute terms
questions.explanation: Surface area still increases, but less than volume, and the distance to the centre increases, so the supply rate per unit volume falls.

questions.text: Proximal convoluted tubule cells have microvilli on the side facing the filtrate and ___ of the membrane on the opposite side, increasing surface area.
questions.explanation: Infolding of the basal membrane increases the area for pumping reabsorbed substances out to the blood; microvilli increase the area for uptake from the filtrate.

questions.prompt: How does flattening help some cells, such as type I pneumocytes, carry out exchange?
options: It decreases surface area to reduce water loss
It increases the volume of cytoplasm
It increases the surface area to volume ratio and shortens the diffusion distance
It allows the cell to store more oxygen
questions.explanation: A flat cell has a large area relative to its volume and is very thin, so gases cross it quickly.

questions.prompt: Which feature of type I pneumocytes adapts them for gas exchange?
options: They are extremely thin, so the diffusion distance between air and blood is very short
They secrete surfactant
They have cilia that move mucus
They contain many mitochondria to pump oxygen
questions.explanation: Type I pneumocytes are about 0.15 µm thick and cover most of the alveolar surface. Gas exchange is passive diffusion, so no pumping is involved.

questions.text: Type II pneumocytes secrete ___, which reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
questions.explanation: Surfactant stops the moist alveolar walls sticking together, so alveoli do not collapse when air is exhaled.

questions.statement: Type II pneumocytes cover most of the alveolar surface.
questions.explanation: Type I pneumocytes cover most of the surface. Type II cells are small cuboidal cells occupying only a small fraction of the area.

questions.prompt: Match each cell to its adaptation.

pairs.right: Very thin, flattened for short diffusion distance
Branched and joined by intercalated discs
Long and multinucleate, formed by cell fusion

questions.explanation: Each cell's structure suits its role: thinness for diffusion, secretory cytoplasm for surfactant, connections for coordinated heartbeats and length for powerful contraction.

questions.prompt: Why do striated muscle fibres contain many nuclei?
options: They are formed by repeated meiosis
Each nucleus controls a different type of contraction
They have lost the ability to make proteins
They form by the fusion of many cells during development
questions.explanation: Embryonic muscle cells fuse into one long fibre, keeping all their nuclei, which supply enough gene expression for such a large volume of cytoplasm.

questions.statement: Striated muscle fibres are sometimes considered an exception to the cell theory because they are far larger than typical cells and have many nuclei.
questions.explanation: A typical cell has one nucleus and is small; muscle fibres share one plasma membrane but contain many nuclei, so it is debatable whether they are single cells.

questions.prompt: What is the role of intercalated discs in cardiac muscle?
options: They store calcium for contraction
They allow electrical impulses to pass rapidly between cells so they contract together
They separate cells so each contracts independently
They attach cardiac muscle to bone
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs contain gap junctions and strong connections, so excitation spreads quickly through the branched network and the heart chamber contracts as a unit.

questions.text: The ___ in the sperm head contains enzymes that digest the zona pellucida surrounding the egg.
questions.explanation: Releasing acrosomal enzymes lets the sperm penetrate the protective layer of glycoproteins around the egg.

questions.prompt: Match each part of a gamete to its adaptation.

pairs.right: Many mitochondria supplying ATP for movement
Propels the sperm towards the egg
Harden the zona pellucida to prevent polyspermy
Nutrient reserves for the early embryo

questions.explanation: Sperm are small and motile with an energy supply; eggs are large and immobile, with nutrients and a mechanism to block entry of more than one sperm.

questions.prompt: Put the events of fertilization in order.
items: Sperm swims to the egg using its flagellum
Acrosome enzymes digest the zona pellucida
Sperm and egg plasma membranes fuse
Cortical granules release their contents, hardening the zona pellucida
questions.explanation: The sperm must reach and penetrate the zona pellucida before membranes fuse; fusion then triggers the cortical reaction that blocks other sperm.
